allrussian_2025_6: Keep track of the clockwise differences between neighbors. Replacing the middle of a, b, c by a−b+c exchanges the two differences a−b and b−c, leaving all the other differences unchanged. Every initial difference is a nonzero number strictly between −1 and 1, so no difference can be an integer at any stage. Two adjacent entries therefore cannot both be integers, and at most 50 of the 100 entries can be integers. The proposed bound of 52 is impossible.
allrussian_2025_9: Take n=4. Each recorded gcd divides two distinct numbers in {1,2,3,4}, so twice the gcd is at most 4. Only the gcds 1 and 2 are possible. The claim requires |4/2+1|=3 distinct gcds, which is impossible.
bmo_2025_1: Every prime p congruent to 3 modulo 4 is good. Pair each nonzero quadratic residue r with p−r, a nonresidue. List the pairs as (r,p−r), putting all pairs whose first element is odd before p itself and those whose first element is even after p. Each pair sums to p and its two elements have opposite parity. Inserting the odd element p at this boundary makes the full list alternate parity. Each partial sum is congruent to a quadratic residue r or to 0. There are infinitely many such primes, so there are infinitely many good integers.
bmosl_NT_2025_6: Each prime p≡2 (mod 3) is orange. The map x↦x³+c permutes the residues modulo p, since cubing is a bijection when gcd(3,p−1)=1. The orbit beginning at 0 has first iterate c and eventually returns to 0, as every orbit of a permutation on a finite set is a cycle. Thus for every c one of the listed terms is divisible by p. There are infinitely many primes congruent to 2 modulo 3, by Dirichlet’s theorem. The claimed finiteness is false.
bulgaria_2025_2: For any coloring, recoloring all the initially white cells gives a connected grid, so f(n)≤n²−n. For any fixed α>2, choose n≥100 with n^(α−2)>3. Then n^α/3>n²>f(n), contradicting the required lower bound.
canada_2025_1: Use three players numbered so that the initial votes are 0→1, 1→2, 2→0. Update in order 0,1,2 in every round. In round one, the votes become 0→2, 1→0, 2→2. In round two, only the vote of 1 changes, to 2. All votes are now for player 2, and the state is fixed, including after the third round.
china_2025_1: Set α=√2, L=5 and x₁=6. The condition on L holds since 2/(√2−1)=2+2√2<5. The successive terms are 6, 4, 5, 7, 4, 5, 7, … . The steps follow by taking the prescribed floors, and the repeated values 4, 5, 7 are distinct. The fundamental period is 3, which refutes the claimed even period.
chinatst_2025_18: Take n=5, so m=3, and let a=b=(0,1,2). The residues within each list are distinct. The off-diagonal sums give exactly {1,2,3}. Their number is 3, whereas n−√n−1/2 is less than 3 because √5>3/2. The proposed upper bound fails.
izho_2025_2: Number the vertices modulo 1001, with the starting vertex numbered 1. Brunno can keep the chip away from multiples of 7. If both proposed destinations x+k and x−k were multiples of 7, then 2x≡0 modulo 7 and hence x≡0 modulo 7, contradicting the current position. Brunno always has an allowed direction avoiding those 143 vertices, so Rose can color at most 858 vertices.
izho_2025_4: Choose the initial numbers to be 1000!, 1000!+1, …, 1000!+998. Every available divisor i divides 1000!, so whichever label is assigned to that number is false. Therefore 999 candies are impossible on this board.
matharena_aime/aime_2025_9: The original parabola is symmetric about the y-axis. Reflecting it across y=−√3x gives the same image as the stated rotation, since the composition of reflections in the y-axis and that line is a 60° counterclockwise rotation. A point on that line lies on both parabolas if it lies on the original. Solving x²−4=−√3x gives the positive root (−√3+√19)/2, and y=(3−√57)/2<0. This fourth-quadrant intersection has y<−2, whereas the claimed value (5−√21)/4 is positive.
matharena_brumo/brumo_2025_8: The first iterate is 2^10·3². If f^j(2025)=2^a·3^b then the next exponents are (2b,a). Two steps therefore double both exponents. The even positive iterates j=2k have exponents (2·2^k,5·2^k). At j=18 the exponent of 2 is only 1024. The even iterates can first meet both bounds at j=20. An odd iterate j=2k+1 has exponents (10·2^k,2·2^k), so the odd iterates can first meet them at j=21. The minimum is 20.
matharena_cmimc/cmimc_2025_27: Set B=(0,0), C=(7,0), A=(a,h), P=(a,p), where a=5/7 and h=20√3/7 by the side lengths. Write B′=(b,0), C′=(c,0). The two circle equations evaluated at x=a have roots h,p, which yields b=a−hp/a and c=a+hp/(7−a). Their centers are (b/2,(h+p)/2) and ((c+7)/2,(h+p)/2). Because B′ and the first center are equidistant from A and X, their line is perpendicular to AX. Likewise C′ and the second center define a perpendicular to AY. Collinearity of A,X,Y forces the two perpendiculars to be parallel. Comparing their vertical components and horizontal components gives c−b=7, so hp=a(7−a). It follows that AP=h−p=7/√3, which is not 3.
matharena_hmmt/hmmt_feb_2025_12: There are C(7,4)=35 ways to remove four pads while keeping both corners. A connection between the corners needs at least four moves, and only five pads remain. Thus a surviving connection must use all five pads along a shortest path. There are exactly C(4,2)=6 shortest paths, one per choice of the order of two upward and two rightward moves. The disconnected cases number 35−6=29, not 26.
matharena_hmmt/hmmt_feb_2025_25: Since X lies on the circle with diameter AP, AX and XP are perpendicular. If XP=5 as claimed, P must be one of the two points X±5u where u is a unit vector perpendicular to AX. More directly, use A′, the point opposite A on the circumcircle. AX is perpendicular to XA′, so X,P,A′ are collinear. The circumradius is 2√3, giving XA′=√(48−25)=√23. Since P is inside ABC and ∠BPC=120°, P lies on the interior-side arc of the circle centered at A′ through B and C, giving A′P=2√3. Consequently XP is either √23−2√3 or √23+2√3, neither of which is 5. In the given interior configuration it is the difference.
nordic_2025_1: Putting x=y=0 yields f(0)^n=2f(0). The only integer solution for n>2 is f(0)=0. Taking y=0 then gives f(x^n)=f(x)^n, and choosing y=x gives f(2x)^n=2f(x)^n. If f(x) were nonzero, the powers of 2 dividing the two sides would have exponents congruent to 0 and 1 modulo n, respectively. Hence f(x)=0 for every x. The zero function works and is unique.
polish_2025_2: Choose n=1, p=5, k=1 and m=2. Then p=2^(2^1)+1 is prime and p divides 2^k−m=0. The proposed universal nondivisibility fails already at l=1 because p² also divides 0. If a nonzero difference is desired, l=21 gives 2^21≡2 modulo 25 by Euler’s theorem.
polish_2025_4: Take n=4 and S={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}. This has exactly 2n elements, all at most n². For r=1 the seven ordered pairs (2,1), (3,2), …, (8,7) all have difference 1. Thus the asserted upper bound of two representations is false.
